86: “Brother dear!” she whispered, pressing him convulsively to her. Then, suddenly tearing herself away, she ran into the gate of her house without looking round.

83: “Don’t bluster, Lukáshka, but listen to me,” she answered, not pulling away her hands but holding the Cossack at arm’s length. “It’s true I am a girl, but you listen to me! It does not depend on me, but if you love me I’ll tell you this. Let go my hands, I’ll tell you without.—I’ll marry you, but you’ll never get any nonsense from me,” said Maryánka without turning her face.
82: The calm expression of Maryánka’s face and voice did not change.
81: “And why keep waiting and waiting? Don’t I love you, darling? You can do what you like with me,” said he suddenly, frowning angrily and seizing both her hands.
80: Lukáshka suddenly clenched his teeth and fists.
79: The girl did not answer. She stood before him breaking her switch into little bits with a rapid movement of her fingers.
78: “Don’t laugh at me, Maryánka! By the Heaven! Well, what if I have a sweetheart? May the devil take her! Only say the word and now I’ll love you—I’ll do anything you wish. 77: “Well, what do you want to say, midnight-gadabout?” and she again began laughing.
76: And freeing herself from his arms she ran away a few steps. When she had reached the wattle fence of her home she stopped and turned to the Cossack who was running beside her and still trying to persuade her to stay a while with him.
75: “What are you talking of, at night time!” answered Maryánka. “Mother is waiting for me, and you’d better go to your sweetheart.”
73: Lukáshka put one arm round her and with the other hand raised her face. “What I wanted to tell you, by Heaven!” his voice trembled and broke.
72: “What an accursed devil! You frightened me! So you have not gone home?” she said, and laughed aloud.
71: The approaching footsteps of a woman attracted his attention. He began listening, and laughed all by himself. Maryánka with bowed head, striking the pales of the fences with a switch, was walking with rapid regular strides straight towards him. Lukáshka rose. Maryánka started and stopped.
70: Meanwhile night had entirely enveloped the village. Bright stars were scattered over the dark sky. The streets became dark and empty. Nazárka remained with the women on the earth-bank and their laughter was still heard, but Lukáshka, having slowly moved away from the girls, crouched down like a cat and then suddenly started running lightly, holding his dagger to steady it: not homeward, however, but towards the cornet’s house. Having passed two streets he turned into a lane and lifting the skirt of his coat sat down on the ground in the shadow of a fence. “A regular cornet’s daughter!” he thought about Maryánka. “Won’t even have a lark—the devil! But just wait a bit.”
69: “I expect I had better go home too, that will be best,” he said, trying to appear unconcerned but hardly able to repress a smile, and he disappeared behind the corner of the house.
68: Lukáshka rose and raised his cap.
67: “I’m coming,” replied the girl. “Go, my dear, go alone—I’ll come in a minute.”
66: “Nursey Maryánka! Hallo Nursey! Mammy is calling! Supper time!” shouted Maryánka’s little brother, running towards the group.
65: Maryánka shook her head, but did so with a smile.
64: “No really ... what I wanted to say to you, ...” whispered Lukáshka. “By the Heavens! Do come!”
63: “I won’t come, I tell you,” Maryánka suddenly said aloud, leaning away from him.
62: “Really I felt so dull all the time without you, I swear I did,” he said in a calm, restrained whisper, helping himself to some seeds out of the bosom of the girl’s smock, and stooping still closer over her he continued with laughing eyes to talk to her in low tones.
60: Maryánka now smiled outright and unfastened the neckband of her smock.
59: “Till the morning. Give me some sunflower seeds,” he said, holding out his hand.
58: “And have you come for long?” asked Maryánka, smiling slightly.
57: “Oh, how glad I am that I got leave from the cordon!” said Lukáshka, moving closer to the girl and looking straight in her eyes all the time.
55: “Do you think I’ve asked?” answered the girl. “I went to get him some chikhir and saw him sitting at the window with Daddy Eróshka. Red-headed he seemed. They’ve brought a whole cartload of things.”
54: “And is he old or young,” asked Lukáshka, sitting down beside her.
53: “We’ve let him have the new hut,” she said.
52: “And where have you put up the chief?” he asked. Maryánka thought for a moment.
51: Lukáshka came slowly up to Maryánka.
50: Again everyone broke into peals of laughter.
49: “What swells!” said Nazárka, “Just like long-skirted choristers,” and he walked a few steps down the road imitating the soldiers.
48: Maryánka began laughing and all the other girls chimed in.
47: The soldiers passed by in silence, keeping step regularly along the dusty road.
46: “People are standing here, so you go round,” he muttered, half turning his head and tossing it contemptuously in the direction of the soldiers.

Nazárka moved, but Lukáshka only screwed up his eyes and turned his broad back without moving from his place.
43: “No, my old one is sweeter,” shouted the Cossack, kissing the struggling old woman.

40: “I’ve heard say they’ll build a bridge across the Térek,” said one of the girls.
39: “Yes, it’s all right for them as they have two huts,” replied an old woman on Maryánka’s behalf, “but at Fómushkin’s now they also have one of the chiefs quartered on them and they say one whole corner is packed full with his things, and the family have no room left. 38: Maryánka, as was her wont, waited before she replied, and slowly raising her eyes looked at the Cossack. Lukáshka’s eyes were laughing as if something special, apart from what was said, was taking place between himself and the girl.
37: “Well, Maryánka! I hear they’ve quartered one of the chiefs on you?” he said, drawing nearer.
36: Lukáshka all this time had stood silently looking at Maryánka. His gaze evidently confused the girl.
35: “Just look, she doesn’t care. She’d howl, Nazárka, eh? Would she?” said Ergushóv.
33: “You’d have howled, I expect,” said Nazárka, laughing.

31: “There, they say girls have no strength, and you nearly killed me.”
30: The Cossack stepped aside and nearly fell.
29: “What are you up to, you beast?” squealed the rosy, round-faced Ústenka, laughing and lifting her arm to hit him.
28: “Tell her,” shouted he. “That’s quite right what Nazárka says; a circular has been sent round. He can read, you know. Quite true!” And he began embracing the next girl.
27: “Now then, you black pitch!” squealed the girl, “I’ll tell your old woman.”
26: Ergushóv burst into a roar of laughter, and seizing the girl nearest to him, he embraced her. “I tell you true.”
25: “And I’ve also heard say that the girls will have to make the soldiers’ beds and offer them chikhir and honey,” said Nazárka, putting one foot forward and tilting his cap like Lukáshka.
24: “You don’t like it?” Ergushóv began again.
23: “I expect they have smoked you out with their tobacco?” asked another woman. “Smoke as much as you like in the yard, I say, but we won’t allow it inside the hut. 22: “Ah, ha! Have you met with trouble?” said Ergushóv.
21: “They’ve sent three of the devils to us,” said one of the women. “Grandad went to the village Elders, but they say nothing can be done.”
20: “And I say so too,” put in the tipsy Ergushóv, laughing. “What a lot of visitors have come,” he added, pointing to a soldier who was passing by. “The soldiers’ vodka is good—I like it.”
19: “Well, God grant you get something good,” said the Cossack; “I’m glad of it, as I’ve just been saying.”
17: “Have you come for long?” asked a woman, breaking the silence.
16: Lukáshka, when he reached the group, slowly raised his cap and stopped in front of the girls. His broad cheekbones and neck were red. He stood and spoke softly and sedately, but in his tranquillity and sedateness there was more of animation and strength than in all Nazárka’s loquacity and bustle. He reminded one of a playful colt that with a snort and a flourish of its tail suddenly stops short and stands as though nailed to the ground with all four feet. Lukáshka stood quietly in front of the girls, his eyes laughed, and he spoke but little as he glanced now at his drunken companions and now at the girls. When Maryánka joined the group he raised his cap with a firm deliberate movement, moved out of her way and then stepped in front of her with one foot a little forward and with his thumbs in his belt, fingering his dagger. Maryánka answered his greeting with a leisurely bow of her head, settled down on the earth-bank, and took some seeds out of the bosom of her smock. Lukáshka, keeping his eyes fixed on Maryánka, slowly cracked seeds and spat out the shells. All were quiet when Maryánka joined the group.
15: “Are you asleep, fair ones?” said Nazárka. “We’ve come from the cordon to drink your health. We’ve already drunk Lukáshka’s health.”
13: Ergushóv roared with laughter and nudged Nazárka. “You’d better sing. And I’ll begin too. I’m clever, I tell you.”

3: “I expect he’ll get a handsome reward,” said one of the women.

0: Meanwhile the tattoo had sounded in the village square. The people had returned from their work. The herd lowed as in clouds of golden dust it crowded at the village gate. The girls and the women hurried through the streets and yards, turning in their cattle. The sun had quite hidden itself behind the distant snowy peaks. One pale bluish shadow spread over land and sky. Above the darkened gardens stars just discernible were kindling, and the sounds were gradually hushed in the village. The cattle having been attended to and left for the night, the women came out and gathered at the corners of the streets and, cracking sunflower seeds with their teeth, settled down on the earthen embankments of the houses. Later on Maryánka, having finished milking the buffalo and the other two cows, also joined one of these groups.
